idiom_name: function* with yield, driven by for...of / next()
implementation_notes: JavaScript bakes laziness into the language: a generator function suspends at yield and resumes on next(), for...of and the spread operator drive it, and any object with Symbol.iterator becomes a lazy source, so an unbounded or streamed sequence is described as ordinary sequential code. A generator object is single-use and not memoized - re-iterate by calling the generator function again - and abandoned generators keep their frame (and captured resources) until return()/throw() or collection; the classic form is still the right model whenever the consumer may stop early.
pitfalls: Generator objects are one-shot: a second for...of over the same object yields nothing with no error, so APIs that iterate twice silently lose elements.
An abandoned generator keeps its execution frame and anything it captured until it is garbage-collected or returned - use try/finally plus generator.return() when the element source owns a resource.
The language will unroll a generator into an array if a materializing operation (spread, Array.from, destructuring) is used, which turns an infinite sequence into an out-of-memory loop.

variants.name: Iterator helpers on a real iterator (ES2025)
variants.implementation_notes: Iterator helpers add the missing adapter vocabulary directly to iterators: map, filter, take, drop, flatMap, reduce and toArray are installed on Iterator instances and applied element by element, so a chain keeps the declarative shape while still pulling from the source (unlike array methods, which materialize). They are lazily evaluated and single-use - the chain wraps the underlying iterator - but require a modern runtime (and the corresponding lib target in TypeScript); use iterator/generator based sources with them, and prefer them over hand-written pull loops when the transformation is a composition.
pitfalls: Helpers are only in recent runtimes/spec editions: on older engines the same code throws a TypeError, and transpilers do not polyfill the prototype methods they cannot see statically.
Iterator helper chains are single-use like the iterator they wrap - storing the chain and consuming it twice yields an empty second pass.
Unlike array methods, helper callbacks are invoked lazily and interleaved with consumption, so side effects in callbacks run in a different order than in the array equivalents.

variants.name: Async generators and for await (ES2018)
variants.idiom_name: async function* with yield, consumed by for await...of
variants.implementation_notes: Async generators extend laziness across await: each yield happens after an awaited operation, and for await...of pulls one element at a time, which gives natural backpressure for streams, sockets and paged APIs (the consumer suspends while awaiting the next element). They are single-use and must be closed explicitly with return()/aclose-like semantics; use a synchronous generator when nothing is awaited, and a queue/stream abstraction when several consumers must share the same source.
pitfalls: An async generator stuck in an await is not cancelled by abandoning the loop: it must be returned/cancelled explicitly, or work continues in the background (unhandled rejection risk).
Single-consumer only: two concurrent for await loops over one async generator split the element stream nondeterministically.
Errors propagate as rejected pulls at the consumer, so the stack points at the loop rather than at the producing code.
